# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Jeong_2024_levocetirizine"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Jeong_2024_levocetirizine"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics16010146>
* Supplement (Supplementary Information 1-8, Tables S1-S8, Figures S1-S6):
  <https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/pharmaceutics16010146/s1>

Jeong 2024 asked whether men and women handle a 5 mg levocetirizine tablet
differently, and whether any difference matters for the drug's antihistamine
effect. Women reached a higher peak and cleared the drug from plasma faster
than men, which the final model attributes to a smaller peripheral volume
(Vp/F) in women, even after body surface area and serum albumin are accounted
for. Total exposure (AUC) was the same in both sexes, and the simulated wheal and
flare suppression differed by only a few percentage points.

The pharmacokinetic model and its covariates come from the authors' own
bioequivalence cohort. The pharmacodynamic model, two parallel
indirect-response models for the histamine-induced skin wheal and flare, was
fitted to published mean data from children aged 6 to 11 years (Simons 2005) and
then linked to the adult PK model. Both layers are in a single model file because
the paper's simulations (Figures 4 and 5, Table 1) drive both PD endpoints from
the one PK model.

# Population

Forty healthy Korean adults (24 men, 16 women) received a single oral 5 mg
levocetirizine tablet (UCB Pharma reference formulation) with 150 mL of water
after a fast of more than 10 h. This was the reference period of a randomised,
open-label, two-way crossover bioequivalence study with a 7-day washout
(Supplementary Information 3). Plasma was sampled at 0, 0.17, 0.33, 0.5, 0.75, 1,
1.25, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 and 36 h post-dose (LLOQ 0.5 ng/mL).

Baseline demographics (Table S1, mean (SD)): age 28.38 (8.30) years; body weight
66.97 (12.59) kg (men 71.58 (12.81), women 60.05 (8.68)); height 168.33 (9.10) cm;
body surface area 1.76 (0.20) m^2 (men 1.85 (0.19), women 1.63 (0.13)); serum
albumin 4.70 (0.24) g/dL (men 4.79 (0.23), women 4.57 (0.17)). Renal and hepatic
function were normal; none of the renal indices survived covariate selection.

The same information is available programmatically via
`readModelDb("Jeong_2024_levocetirizine")()$population`.

# Virtual cohort

The individual data are not published, so the checks below use a virtual
cohort of 100 men and 100 women, sampled on the paper's 16-point schedule.
Height, weight and albumin are drawn per sex from the Table S1 means and SDs;
BSA is then computed with the Mosteller formula the paper used
(Supplementary Information 1).

```{r cohort}
# set.seed() fixes the covariate draws. rxSetSeed() fixes rxode2's random
# effects for a given solver thread count but not across thread counts, so
# every assertion on this stochastic cohort below uses a robust centre with a
# generous envelope; the tight assertions run on typical-value solves.
set.seed(20240121)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20240121)

sampling_times <- c(0, 0.17, 0.33, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36)

make_cohort <- function(n, sexf, ht, ht_sd, wt, wt_sd, wt_min, alb, alb_sd,
                        label, id_offset = 0L) {
  subjects <- tibble(
    id = id_offset + seq_len(n),
    SEXF = sexf,
    HT = stats::rnorm(n, ht, ht_sd),
    WT = pmax(stats::rnorm(n, wt, wt_sd), wt_min),
    # Table S1 albumin is in g/dL; the model's ALB column is g/L.
    ALB = 10 * stats::rnorm(n, alb, alb_sd),
    treatment = label
  ) |>
    mutate(BSA = sqrt(HT * WT / 3600))
  doses <- subjects |>
    mutate(time = 0, amt = 5, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot", dvid = NA_integer_)
  obs <- subjects |>
    tidyr::expand_grid(time = sampling_times) |>
    mutate(amt = NA_real_, evid = 0L, cmt = "central", dvid = 1L)
  bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
}

events <- bind_rows(
  make_cohort(100, 0, 173.41, 7.50, 71.58, 12.81, 50, 4.79, 0.23, "Male", 0L),
  make_cohort(100, 1, 160.70, 5.08, 60.05, 8.68, 45, 4.57, 0.17, "Female", 100L)
)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(events[, c("id", "time", "evid")]))

events |>
  distinct(id, treatment, WT, BSA, ALB) |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(across(c(WT, BSA, ALB), \(x) round(mean(x), 2)), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::rename(
    Sex = treatment, "Mean WT (kg)" = WT, "Mean BSA (m^2)" = BSA,
    "Mean ALB (g/L)" = ALB
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Virtual-cohort covariate means (Table S1: men 71.58 kg, 1.85 m^2, 47.9 g/L; women 60.05 kg, 1.63 m^2, 45.7 g/L).")
```

# Simulation

The model has three endpoints (plasma `Cc`, `wheal` and `flare`), so
observation rows carry `dvid = 1L` to tie them to the first endpoint; the
wheal and flare states are returned as columns at the same rows.

```{r simulate}
mod <- readModelDb("Jeong_2024_levocetirizine")

sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod,
  events = events,
  keep = c("treatment"),
  useLinCmt = FALSE
) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

Typical-value solves use the per-sex mean covariates from Table S1, as the
paper did for Table 1 and Figures 4D-4F and 5D-5F ("applying the mean
biochemical parameter values in each gender").

```{r simulate-typical}
mod_typical <- mod |> rxode2::zeroRe()

sex_covariates <- tibble(
  treatment = c("Male", "Female"),
  SEXF = c(0, 1),
  WT = c(71.58, 60.05),
  BSA = c(1.85, 1.63),
  ALB = c(47.9, 45.7)
)

typical_solve <- function(times, n_doses = 1L, tau = 24) {
  rows <- bind_rows(
    tibble(time = 0, amt = 5, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot",
           ii = if (n_doses > 1L) tau else 0, addl = n_doses - 1L,
           dvid = NA_integer_),
    tibble(time = times, amt = NA_real_, evid = 0L, cmt = "central",
           ii = 0, addl = 0L, dvid = 1L)
  )
  ev <- dplyr::cross_join(sex_covariates |> mutate(id = row_number()), rows) |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
  rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typical, ev, keep = "treatment", useLinCmt = FALSE) |>
    as.data.frame()
}

typical_sd <- typical_solve(seq(0, 36, by = 0.01))
typical_md <- typical_solve(seq(0, 240, by = 0.01), n_doses = 10L)
```

# Table 1 of the paper

Table 1 reports typical-value simulations at the per-sex mean covariates, for a
single dose (0-36 h) and at steady state (216-240 h, once daily). The rows are
recomputed below with the paper's definitions: the minimum is taken after the
peak (footnote a), the wheal and flare maxima after the maximum effect
(footnote b), the fluctuation is maximum / minimum (footnote d), and the
single-dose AUEC is the area between the 100% baseline and the response curve.

```{r table-1}
window_metrics <- function(d) {
  d <- arrange(d, time)
  trap <- function(y) sum(diff(d$time) * (head(y, -1) + tail(y, -1)) / 2)
  dur <- diff(range(d$time))
  after <- function(y, i) y[i:length(y)]
  i_c <- which.max(d$Cc)
  i_w <- which.min(d$wheal)
  i_f <- which.min(d$flare)
  tibble(
    metric = c(
      "Cc maximum", "Cc minimum", "Cc mean", "Cc AUCall",
      "Wheal maximum", "Wheal minimum", "Wheal mean", "Wheal AUEC",
      "Flare maximum", "Flare minimum", "Flare mean", "Flare AUEC"
    ),
    value = c(
      max(d$Cc), min(after(d$Cc, i_c)), trap(d$Cc) / dur, trap(d$Cc),
      max(after(d$wheal, i_w)), min(d$wheal), trap(d$wheal) / dur,
      trap(100 - d$wheal),
      max(after(d$flare, i_f)), min(d$flare), trap(d$flare) / dur,
      trap(100 - d$flare)
    )
  )
}

simulated_t1 <- bind_rows(
  typical_sd |> group_by(treatment) |>
    reframe(window_metrics(pick(everything()))) |> mutate(period = "Single dose"),
  typical_md |> filter(time >= 216) |> group_by(treatment) |>
    reframe(window_metrics(pick(everything()))) |> mutate(period = "Steady state")
)

# Jeong 2024 Table 1. The steady-state AUEC rows are omitted: their values
# (2431.14 and 3517.14 h*% in men) are inconsistent with a 24 h window around
# the reported steady-state means, so the integration window is unclear.
published_t1 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~period, ~metric, ~Male, ~Female,
  "Single dose", "Cc maximum", 212.00, 220.52,
  "Single dose", "Cc minimum", 6.53, 4.39,
  "Single dose", "Cc mean", 45.15, 46.09,
  "Single dose", "Cc AUCall", 1624.90, 1659.09,
  "Single dose", "Wheal maximum", 89.45, 92.77,
  "Single dose", "Wheal minimum", 33.81, 31.87,
  "Single dose", "Wheal mean", 63.02, 64.30,
  "Single dose", "Wheal AUEC", 1330.75, 1284.66,
  "Single dose", "Flare maximum", 72.56, 87.14,
  "Single dose", "Flare minimum", 0.77, 0.65,
  "Single dose", "Flare mean", 20.31, 25.93,
  "Single dose", "Flare AUEC", 2867.43, 2665.73,
  "Steady state", "Cc maximum", 231.37, 235.37,
  "Steady state", "Cc minimum", 20.69, 16.19,
  "Steady state", "Cc mean", 70.73, 70.71,
  "Steady state", "Cc AUCall", 1702.49, 1702.49,
  "Steady state", "Wheal maximum", 70.81, 75.54,
  "Steady state", "Wheal minimum", 30.17, 29.39,
  "Steady state", "Wheal mean", 48.79, 50.22,
  "Steady state", "Flare maximum", 13.11, 21.10,
  "Steady state", "Flare minimum", 0.44, 0.43,
  "Steady state", "Flare mean", 3.49, 5.05
) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Male, Female), names_to = "treatment", values_to = "published")

t1 <- inner_join(published_t1, simulated_t1, by = c("period", "metric", "treatment")) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (value - published) / published)
stopifnot(nrow(t1) == nrow(published_t1))

t1 |>
  mutate(across(c(published, value, pct_diff), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  select(period, metric, treatment, published, value, pct_diff) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    Period = period, Quantity = metric, Sex = treatment,
    "Jeong 2024 Table 1" = published, Simulated = value, "% difference" = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Typical-value reproduction of Jeong 2024 Table 1 (concentrations in ng/mL, AUC in h*ng/mL, PD in % of baseline, AUEC in h*%).")
```

These are deterministic solves, so the gates below are tight. The structural
quantities (peak, mean, AUC, the whole wheal response) agree within 5%. The
remaining gap, largest for the post-peak minimum and the low flare values, comes
from the unreported covariate medians (see Assumptions): the medians move the
male and female Vp/F, and so the terminal phase, in opposite directions. A
mis-transcribed volume, clearance or IC50 would move these rows by tens of
percent.

```{r table-1-gate}
gate <- t1 |>
  mutate(bound = case_when(
    metric == "Cc minimum" ~ 15,
    startsWith(metric, "Flare") ~ 20,
    TRUE ~ 5
  ))
stopifnot(all(abs(gate$pct_diff) < gate$bound))

# Steady-state AUC over a dosing interval equals Dose / (CL/F) exactly for a
# linear model: 5 mg / 2.94 L/h = 1700.68 h*ng/mL. Both sides use the same
# parameters, so the bound is numerical error only.
auc_ss <- t1 |> filter(period == "Steady state", metric == "Cc AUCall") |> pull(value)
stopifnot(all(abs(auc_ss / (5000 / 2.94) - 1) < 1e-3))

# Drug-free PD baseline is kin / kout = 100 for both endpoints.
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(typical_sd$wheal[typical_sd$time == 0], c(100, 100))),
  isTRUE(all.equal(typical_sd$flare[typical_sd$time == 0], c(100, 100)))
)
```

# PKNCA validation

```{r pknca}
sim_nca <- sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, treatment)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(sim_nca, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)

dose_df <- events |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, amt, treatment)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id)

intervals <- data.frame(
  start = 0,
  end = Inf,
  cmax = TRUE,
  tmax = TRUE,
  auclast = TRUE,
  aucinf.obs = TRUE,
  half.life = TRUE
)

nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(
  PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals)
)
```

## Comparison against published NCA

```{r nca-compare}
# Jeong 2024 Table S2, observed mean by sex (AUCall over 0-36 h is auclast).
published <- tibble::tribble(
  ~treatment, ~cmax, ~tmax, ~auclast, ~aucinf.obs, ~half.life,
  "Male", 203.89, 1.11, 1647.94, 1751.08, 8.73,
  "Female", 230.84, 1.09, 1783.22, 1835.06, 7.05
)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca_res,
  reference = published,
  by = "treatment",
  units = c(
    cmax = "ng/mL", auclast = "ng*h/mL", aucinf.obs = "ng*h/mL",
    tmax = "h", half.life = "h"
  ),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)

knitr::kable(
  cmp,
  caption = "Simulated (median of 100 subjects per sex) vs. Jeong 2024 Table S2 (observed mean). * differs from reference by >20%.",
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

AUC and half-life agree with the observed means, and the model reproduces the
sex ordering the paper reports: women have the higher Cmax and the shorter
half-life.

**Cmax and Tmax in the stochastic cohort.** The simulated Cmax is about 15-20%
below the observed mean and Tmax is later, although the typical-value Cmax
reproduces Table 1 within 4%. The cause is the published inter-individual
variability on the four fast absorption rate constants (omega^2 2.09 to 4.14,
i.e. SDs of 1.4 to 2.0 on the log scale) and on Vc/F (0.89). A sizeable minority
of simulated subjects therefore absorb slowly or have a large central volume,
which pulls the cohort peak down and spreads it out in time. The paper's own
visual predictive check shows the same thing: in Figure 2A the predicted 2.5th
percentile over the first hours lies well below every observation. The simulated
percentiles of the virtual cohort agree with the prediction lines read from
Figure 2A (on the natural-log scale, a median of about 4.0 at 12 h and 1.8 at
36 h, and a 2.5th percentile of about 0.3 at 36 h). This is a property of the
published model and is reproduced as published; no parameter was changed.

```{r check-cohort}
# Stochastic cohort: assert the centre of the exposure and elimination
# quantities against the published means, with an envelope wide enough for any
# cohort the model can draw. A wrong clearance, volume or unit moves these by
# far more than 25%. Cmax and Tmax are not gated, for the reason given above.
nca_summary <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result) |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("aucinf.obs", "half.life")) |>
  group_by(treatment, PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(median = median(PPORRES, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(
    published |>
      select(treatment, aucinf.obs, half.life) |>
      pivot_longer(-treatment, names_to = "PPTESTCD", values_to = "ref"),
    by = c("treatment", "PPTESTCD")
  )
stopifnot(nrow(nca_summary) == 4, all(abs(nca_summary$median / nca_summary$ref - 1) < 0.25))
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Covariate centring values are the cohort means, not the medians.**
  Supplementary Information 7 centres weight, BSA and albumin on "the median ...
  values in the observed population", but Table S1 reports only means and SDs.
  The model uses the Table S1 means (66.97 kg, 1.76 m^2, 4.70 g/dL). With these
  centres the typical-value reproduction of Table 1 is within 5% for Cmax, AUC,
  mean concentration and all wheal quantities. The post-peak minimum (up to
  13% off) and the low-valued flare rows (up to 16% off) are the most sensitive
  to the true medians. No centre was tuned to match the table.
* **Albumin is supplied in g/L.** The paper reports albumin in g/dL; the
  canonical `ALB` column is g/L, so the centre is 47.0 g/L. The ratio form makes
  the effect unit-invariant once the centre is converted as well.
* **The weight covariate acts on Ka5, not Ka4.** Table S7 footnote c says
  "the quantitative correlation value between Ka4 and body weight", but the
  printed equation (Supplementary Information 7 Eq. 5), the covariate table
  (Table S6 model 5), the Results and the Conclusions all place it on Ka5. The
  model follows the equation.
* **`omega^2` for Vp/F and CLp/F is encoded as `fixed(0)`.** Table S7 prints
  both as 0.00 (bootstrap 0.00-0.00), while Table S5 shows that removing either
  worsened the fit by more than 400 units of -2LL. The variances are therefore
  non-zero but below the two-decimal reporting precision; they are carried as
  explicit zeros rather than invented.
* **The residual-error model is "log additive" in Phoenix NLME**, i.e. additive
  on the natural-log scale, which is log-normal on the linear concentration
  scale and maps to `~ lnorm(expSd)`. Table S7 reports epsilon = 0.11; Phoenix
  reports this parameter as a standard deviation.
* **The PD sub-model has no IIV and no residual error.** Table S8 gives point
  estimates only; `addSd_wheal` and `addSd_flare` are `fixed(0)`.
* **The PD data are not from this cohort.** The wheal and flare responses were
  taken from Simons 2005 (children aged 6 to 11 years given 5 mg levocetirizine)
  and fitted with the adult PK structure (Methods 2.4). The authors note that
  adult PD studies are needed to confirm the parameters (Discussion).
* **Response scale.** Supplementary Information 8 calls R the "percent
  inhibition" of the wheal or flare, but Table 1 and Figures 3-5 plot it as the
  response size relative to a 100% baseline that falls towards 0 as the
  antihistamine effect grows, which is what `kin / kout = 100` gives. The model
  follows the plotted scale.
* **The stochastic cohort's Cmax is lower and its Tmax later than observed.**
  This follows from the large published IIV on Ka1-Ka4 and Vc/F and matches
  the width of the paper's own VPC (Figure 2); see the PKNCA section.
* **Steady-state AUEC is not compared.** Table 1 reports 2431.14 and
  3517.14 h*% (men, wheal and flare) at steady state, which cannot come from a
  24 h window around steady-state mean responses of 48.79% and 3.49%; the
  integration window used is not stated.
* **Virtual-cohort covariates are assumed normal and independent within sex**
  (height, weight, albumin), with BSA computed from height and weight. The paper
  publishes summary statistics only.
